text_fidelity_a:
Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black I lived and breathed full-sized Kensington trackball mice from about 1987 until my last one stopped functioning and I couldn't find them anymore...probably in the late '90s. Tried some others; all had small, lightweight balls that gave none of the feel and control of Kensinton's...Expert Mouse? Was that what it was called back then too? Because it was the same general design as the current Expert Mouse, but the body was computer-case white.

Anyway, I had several of those (the quality going downhill with each iteration, as I recall) and loved them, and since they disappeared (as far as I could tell), I adapted, first to trackpads, which I've never liked much, and then back to traditional mice which don't give nearly the control of a trackball. Now, at last, it seems Kensington has again begun to produce truly worthwhile trackball mice, and this is one. Oh, it's _so_ good to have one of these again.

I'm doing that thing I hate when other people do it and reviewing the product as soon as I've gotten it up and running, without any kind of experiential history behind my assessment. I'll come back and update this in the future if necessary. But so far: I'm happy, happy, happy to have a real, full-sized Kensington trackball mouse again, with a heavy, substantial ball. There are only two things about this device that I'm not crazy about: In my old Kensington mice, the ball rested on physical rollers and I could give the ball a good spin and it would keep spinning for a second before stopping; it spun much more freely in its cavity than this ball does (so far...maybe that's something that will break in?) [Update: yes, after about three days of use the ball rolls more smoothly and silently than the old one on rollers ever did]. And the other thing is the scrolling mechanism. It's weird. Despite the KensingtonWorks software trying to make us believe otherwise, the "scroll ring" itself actually has nothing to do with scrolling, nor with anything else - the "scroll ring" is not even a control, but just a static piece of chrome trim. What makes the mouse scroll is twisting the ball this way or that from the top, as if it were a knob. At first I thought the "scroll ring" wasn't working because I was trying to use it without touching the ball...which does nothing. And now that I've figured out how scrolling works (you rest your finger on the "scroll ring" and push and pull the side of the ball)...I'm not crazy about it. I'm getting used to it, but it's just a weird way to scroll (I can't for the life of me remember how I used to do it on the Expert Mouse decades ago). It does work though.

(Update on the scrolling: I'm also not crazy about the way the KensingtonWorks software handles the scrolling speed adjustment. When you make the base pointer movement speed faster, the pointer continues to move smoothly, but just faster. When you make the scrolling speed faster though, you lose all smoothness - the software makes the scrolling faster by breaking it into successively larger and more jarring jumps. At the slowest speed, it's pretty smooth; at the highest speeds it's no longer really scrolling, but simply jumping abruptly from one screenful (or page) to the next. Increasing the scrolling speed just increases the size of these jumps, but I find them jarring and annoying starting at the second or third lowest speed setting.)

I also had to figure out how to program one of the buttons as a click lock, since Kensington doesn't call it that anymore, but calls it "left drag", "right drag", and "middle drag" (and I have no idea what the difference is between those three - I just chose "left drag" and it's working fine).

So far, those are my only gripes, all minor. So happy to have one of these things again! =) (Did I mention that?)

Enjoy...
text_fidelity_b: Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red) This camera is what I call a "subcompact" - the smallest point and shoot cameras that have vertically mounted lenses which allow protection, compactness, and quicker start up times. Normally, you'd expect a small trade off for these features, so I wouldn't compare this directly with a camera endowed by a telescoping lens.

Sony invented the subcompact with the T1 a few years back (at least in my world), and I was able to compare the FinePix Z90 with the one-generation-older 12 MP Sony T90. I'll go the pro/con route...

PROS of the Z90:

-Price is something like half of the latest subcompact Sony.
-Operational costs are cheaper: USB cable is non-proprietary (in case you want a second one or need to replace it) and SD card is cheaper and more universal than Sony's Memory Stick.
-Separate physical buttons to record movies and to take pictures. This is genius to me, because I hate to miss a great video opportunity while fumbling through the menus.
-Does not come with a memory card, BUT cameras that do usually come with one so small that it is worthless. Internal memory is better, because it allows you to copy from one camera card to another, which can be useful.
-Can set it up to take two photos at once, with and without the flash. As an amateur, I often do this manually anyway, but this way you get closer photos (chronologically)to compare in a dynamic scenario, and the subject needs only to pose once.
-The panorama mode works better than in other cameras I've used. They use internal weights alla smart phones (I'm guessing) to help you line up the next picture. Allows you to "pan" a panorama shot in play mode.
-There is a time zone mode that allows you to temporarily change the time (for timestamps).
-The display changes from horizontal to vertical as you move the camera respectively.
-"Touch and track" mode follows a subject.
-Side by side picture compare.
-Search by face, couple, group, favorites, scene, or date, and view a small picture next to thumbnails.
-Charger is smaller with the plug offset to allow it to use only one receptacle on a power strip (as long as it is at the end of said strip).

CONS of the Z90:

-Picture quality was not as good as the Sony 80% of the time (tested in various modes and lighting conditions). That said, a tripod really helps with low light and no flash, where both cameras struggle without it.
-By numbers, it is not much larger than the Sony, but it feels significantly larger.
-Sometimes the "buttons" in the corners of the touch screen need to be pressed more than once.
-Tripod mount has plastic threads, instead of a machined metal insert.
-Cannot take shots as rapidly as on the Sony
-Does not tell you what zoom level you are at. 5x zoom does not appear to make a great difference over 4x.
-"play" and "camera" buttons could be one button used as a toggle.
-Battery can be put in backward, as the slot is not keyed (although the battery is). No big deal, but shows something wasn't thought out thoroughly.

Bottom Line:

The Fuji is trying to deliver everything the market leader has to offer for a much more manageable price tag. It gets an A for effort, delivering a lot of great menu options, and may actually win in that respect, but the picture quality is not as good. If they could pour a little more money into the actual optics and the touch screen and still keep the price reasonable, they might win the battle in the future. For now, it's purely a personal budget vs. quality decision.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red)

StarTech.com StarTech.com 1-Port 10/100 Mbps Parallel Network Print Server - Fast Centronics Ethernet Printer Server Adapter - Windows 10 (PM1115P2) Customer service is 6 stars

I certainly would love this product if we could have gotten it to work. I'm on a 5GB wifi network, and the StarTech is for a 2.4GB network. It won't work with my Internet speed. Or so both my techie, Brian, and I thought. Keep reading.

However... I couldn't connect the print server (that's the little white box) with my laptop. I had a problem and got online to get it fixed. The chat tech was very polite, patient and knowledgeable, but pointed me to the support page that gave me step by step how to set up my wifi print server. Went there. Followed the steps but I had no idea what the server IP address was. Gave up until I could call and get someone to walk me through it. A survey came up asking for my thoughts on my experience. I told them I was having a problem and just needed to know what my server IP address was so I could set up to print from my laptop. Got an email from a supervisor asking if I'd like a more experienced tech to call me. Yes! I would.

Got a call from Brian. He was very helpful, patient, and walked me through everything. Then I had to let him have remote control over the process because it got too complicated for me. That's when we discovered that the print server wouldn't work with my internet speed. So I told him how grateful I was for his patience and help even though I couldn't use the thing that was going to save me so much time. We hung up and while I was typing up this 6-star review of StarTech's great tech support, Brian called me back and said he was pretty sure he'd figured it out. I gave him remote control again, and 15 minutes later I've got my wonderful wifi printer!! I'm so elated! It works.

I have Windows 10 OS on my Dell Inspiron laptop, and an HP J4540 printer -- 2008. They are now friends and talking to each other wirelessly.

I do not recommend anyone that does not know what they are doing to install this device themselves. I know a lot about computers, but I know when I need an expert. Brian is an expert! Installing the thing is complicated. If your wifi is 2.4GB, then you can follow the instructions on the website most likely without a problem. If you have a higher speed Internet, then there's a lot more backdoor stuff that needs doing. I have a feeling they'll be updating the instructions on the website for this kind of problem. But if you have any problems, contact StarTech tech support. They are the greatest this side of the sun... no joke!

Samsung Gear IconX (2018 Edition) SM-R140NZKAXAR Bluetooth Cord-free Fitness Earbuds, w/ On-board 4Gb MP3 Player (US Version with Warranty) - Black I’m NOT an audiophile, but I was blown away by the sound quality delivered by these SAMSUNG GEAR ICONX (2018 Edition) BLUETOOTH CORD-FREE FITNESS EARBUDS (w/On-board 4Gb MP3 Player; Gray (SM-R140NZAAXAR)). I like classical music, and the sound is so relaxing and immersive, I forget that I’m wearing earbuds. (It helps that these are totally without wires, of course.)

The earbuds are far and away the most comfortable that I’ve ever worn. You get three sizes of in-ear tips (S, M, L). There is NO sound leakage to speak of. The touch controls for music work fine, though it takes some practice to master the double- and triple-taps (sound tracks) and swipes (volume) so that you get consistent results. For me, it’s easiest to play an album or list at a set volume, without fussing with the controls.

I didn’t test the call-answering features or other features beyond playing music. The earbuds paired, without incident, with my iPad Pro and with my Samsung Galaxy S7 Edge. The charging case seems to need to be charged up to the green light for pairing to work.

A great feature is that you can copy music files to the earbuds. They have 4GB of built-in storage. This means you don’t have to stay within Bluetooth range of your mobile device to play music.

Three stars because I haven’t used the earbuds consistently for a full month. As much as I love these, I’m afraid that the left earbud will fail before long (as other reviewers have reported).

Already the left earbud has exhibited signs of NOT charging properly. With the case closed and plugged in (and with brand-new earbuds), the left charging light blinked red, which indicates “not charging”. I corrected the problem by opening the case and reseating the left earbud in the cradle, but of course I’m wondering whether there is a more serious problem that will surface soon.

text_fidelity_a:
ECLIPSE PHOTO GROUP Front and Rear Professional Lens Protectors As someone who works with cameras for a living, I tend to occasionally misplace/lose my lens caps. Having a one-size-fits-all backup like this claims to be, is therefore intriguing to me.
What I found however, is that this fits alright for smaller sized primes (such as those with a front element of 52mm), but a lot of my zooms or larger primes with bigger front elements are difficult or impossible to fit over. Rear cap was also somewhat of a hit-or-miss; I own E-mount, EOS, Nikon F, Minolta A-mount and Micro4/3 lenses, and none of them are too large in their rear element, but some lenses get wide right after the mount and won't allow a cover like this to squeeze over easily. Some of the smaller primes, especially pancake lenses like the Canon 40mm STM, really can't fit both a front and rear "cap" like this since the entire lens would be engulfed in one end or the other.
On top of all that, even if it DOES fit over your lens, I'm cynical as to how how useful it really is. The purpose of a lens cap is to protect the glass from two things: getting dirty and getting damaged. For starters, the material is soft and won't prevent a hard object collision. I'm not exactly willing to test that theory but considering I can press in and feel the glass through the cover, I'm guessing a hard object in your camera bag could still hit it and crack/shatter/damage it. Perhaps the rubber would soften the blow, but a real lens cap would prevent any blow from happening in the first place!
For dust and debris protection, perhaps it is a little useful, however this sort of material tends to attract a lot of static cling. Just leaving it in my gear bag for a bit, I'm finding dust and hair clinging to it like a balloon. Now, it is possible that means the dust/debris will stick to the cap and not your lens, which is useful, however it doesn't give me a lot of confidence to see stuff stuck to the thing I'm about to use to protect my lens from more of that stuff.

I suppose it's good as a backup in my gearbag in case I lose another lens cap and want something to keep dust off it until I get a replacement, but otherwise I'd strongly recommend getting a proper front and end cap for your lenses.
text_fidelity_b: ECLIPSE PHOTO GROUP Front and Rear Professional Lens Protectors

text_fidelity_a:
CableMod C-Series Classic ModMesh Sleeved Cable Kit for Corsair Type 4 RM Black Label/RMi/RMX (White) I purchased these for the RM650x in my new build. to clean up the appearance of my case, as the default Corsair cables are serviceable but neither flexible nor visually appealing. Do I have a fancy case? It's a Fractal Define Mini C, so, sorta. Do I have a side window? No. Will anyone ever see the interior of this case aside from me and randos and I'm flexing on? Certainly not.

Why get cables like these? Call it an eccentricity. I don't like chaos hiding right out of sight. Sure, the Mini C would have the outward appearance of a stocky monolith of unalloyed order, but inside there would be a twisting madness of PVC and copper, heaving silently against the surface. There would be no evidence of it, sure, but I would know.

I would know.

So anyway, I purchased these to extend the relentless teleology of the IC into the broader world, and to this end I was successful. The cables are much more flexible than the default ones and the paracord is an interesting contrast against the typical circuit boards and enameled aluminum panels. They are a bit pricey for what you get, that's definitely the case - you might be better served by getting a different brand or shorter extensions rather than the full PSU set. I just happened to have the money for the CableMods.

Caveats: if you are using velcro ties inside the case, then you have to be careful with the ModFlex, as the hook-side can pull threads from it. I presume ModMesh, being nylon, would not have that issue. to get around it, I used rubber/silicon bands, since unlike zipties they can be removed and adjusted relatively easily.

Would I recommend them? If you have a side-window or transparent case, they are a definitely aesthetically on point. ModFlex or ModMesh, either should be suitable. If not, unless you too are eccentric, it probably isn't worth it. The improvement in airflow and the reduction in strain on the components are minimal so long as you are implementing reasonable cable management techniques. I'm still happy I purchased them though, since I'm pretty sure I'll be able to use them in the next two-three builds and they did make it a bit easier to get everything where I wanted it.
text_fidelity_b: CableMod C-Series Classic ModMesh Sleeved Cable Kit for Corsair Type 4 RM Black Label/RMi/RMX (White)

Garmin nüvi 1350LMT 4.3-Inch Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)) I drive in and around the Boston area, where none of the streets run north/south or east/west, every other intersection is a rotary, and a wrong turn down a one way street can take you an hour to correct.

The Nuvi is slightly better than trying to drive with a map on your steering wheel. I have been using mine for awhile now, and it mostly gets me where I want to go.

The problem is mostly how it does it. As many have already noted, there is no easy way to get it to show you alternate routes. And out of the city, especially, the route it gives you can be full of surprises. Take you off the highway and onto a dirt road for no reason whatsoever surprises. That happened to my husband on his way to a job in Hartford.

And forget trying to get around traffic. I was using it to get home from a doctor's office and saw that there was a ton of traffic on the route it was giving me through Harvard Square, so I turned toward another way home - one I do not know as well, but I know it is possible to get home that way - expecting the Nuvi to tell me it was recalculating and give me my next turn.

PreSonus C3.5 BT Channel Studio Monitor I have been wanting to get a bluetooth speaker for connecting to my tablet for a while so I was very pleased to get an opportunity to try this speaker set. It is far and away better than what I originally had in mind and so far I am more than pleased with them.

Setup of these speakers is straightforward and simple, so much so that instructions really are not needed to get started. The wire connector is color-coded to make connecting the speakers to each other almost completely foolproof. If I have any complaints about the setup it would be that the wire connector is a little on the short side but that’s an easy fix - just buy longer wire.

I enabled bluetooth on my tablet, told the speaker set to make itself available and the tablet connected to it immediately. One could not ask for anything simpler. The process took less than a minute and most of that time was spent walking across the room to press the bluetooth button on the speakers.

I loaded up Pandora and told the tablet to play and almost immediately it was clear that these speakers are far above average. The sound profile is stunning - clear and crisp highs, rich midrange and very satisfying bass without overdriving. These speakers do an outstanding job of accurately reproducing the sound. On the back of the main (control) speaker there are two knobs for adjusting the highs and lows should the middle be unsatisfactory for some reason. These speakers also do a good job with spacial elements and there is depth to the sound.

I paired the speakers with my laptop (once I powered off the tablet) as well and it was also very easy.

I took some cables and wired the speakers to an older television in the house to see how much better watching TV would be. It was definitely better and it have a more spacial and stereo sound experience but with our TV this prevented us from making any volume adjustments unless we turned the volume knob on the speaker itself. This is a minor nuisance but certainly not a real issue.

In addition to great sound, these seem to be well-build and rugged, a good sign right out of the box. These are an excellent choice for a home theater system or an audiophile's listening room.

So far I have found nothing about which to complain with these speakers. Set-up is a snap and the sound quality is just amazing. These are speakers for the serious listener.

LotFancy Laptop Cooler Cooling Pad with 5 Quiet Fans for 12-17" Notebook, Dual USB Ports A good laptop chiller pad becomes important when you run a lot of graphics-intensive games or if you are doing anything requiring the CPU to run a heavy load. Heat is the enemy of a computer system and the fastest way to a dead laptop is to not deal with heat issues when there’s a problem. I had a chill pad some time ago and it was sub-par. This one by LotFancy is much better and it does a good job.

First off, this is a big chill pad, the same basic dimensions as my laptop but much thicker. I have a 15.6" laptop and this pad is almost a perfect and exact fit, with only a narrow area in the back that extends past the end of the laptop. If you want a small and petite chill pad, this is not the one you want. It does incline too with a metal bar and slots in the case so that the laptop can be angled up. This actually is good for exposing it to even more air.

This chill pad connects to a USB port so it can either be plugged into a port on the computer or into a hub. There are two ports on it and both seem to be the same in terms of how the pad operates. That is, the pad operates at the same speed regardless of which port is used. There are also two buttons on the pad for turning it on. One turns on the larger fan in the middle, and the other turns on all the other fans. Two green LEDs next to those buttons indicate that the pad is powered on and working.

This pad moves a lot of air and it does a good job of cooling the laptop. But, it does so very quietly which is a huge plus. I have it set up in my home office and the pad makes about as much noise as a desktop computer, maybe a little less. The sound it makes is a gentle hum.

When powered on each fan has a bright blue LED in it. While they look cool when there’s no laptop on the pad, they’re all but invisible when the laptop is sitting on top. There isn’t even much of a glow coming from the pad. I turned on the pad, turned out all of the lights and the glow from the laptop screen was enough to overpower any light that might have come from the pad. Except for the low hum I wouldn’t know it was even turned on.

This is a good chill pad. It works quietly and it moves a lot of air. Compared to other chill pads I have used this one is very good and I am happy to recommend it.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.
text_fidelity_b: LotFancy Laptop Cooler Cooling Pad with 5 Quiet Fans for 12-17" Notebook, Dual USB Ports

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech C922x Pro + Logitech for Creators Litra Glow - The Ultimate Solution for a Professional Look During Video-Calls I am comparing this to a Logitech C910 HD 1080p webcam which I've been using almost daily since 2012.

I don't stream games but I stream my live DJ broadcasts. I use 4 webcams and a green screen. I use xSplit exclusively.

This C922x Pro Stream is for gamers so they can stream on Twitch or YouTube. The camera is supposed to automatically load a background removing program so you don't have to use a green screen. This special software, Personify ChromaCam, is free when have the C922. Installing is another matter entirely. Myself, like others, have older, but capable systems that cannot install this software. I checked on Personify's website and the PC requirements are: Processor: Intel 4th generation or higher Core CPU, or the AMD equivalent (Quad core AMD Phenom), OS: Windows 7, 8, 10, and Memory: 4GB+ RAM. My system, even though its 3 years old, meets all these specs but when installing I get a 'unable to install due to ABX or ADX" something.

The camera's clarity is not any better than my 4 year old C910. In fact, my C910 has Carl Zeiss, the new cam doesn't not. The colors appear washed out with too much brightness. I expected better, but the C922 regressed a bit in the lens department.

Now here's a kicker for you...you cannot, and I mean, cannot, view the camera while changing it's settings. Yes, you heard me right. Open the camera settings and you get a windowed box for changing the settings, but the webcam does not come on or is it viewable. So, am I supposed to change the settings, open the cam, close the cam, change the settings, open the cam...etc..etc?

The mount is sturdy and multi-positional. I like the added tripod adapter. At this price point there should be a privacy shield.

I had an issue getting the camera to initially turn on. The outer ring would flash but no camera picture. Then I realized that some webcams don't like being plugged into a USB hub. After adding an extension cord and plugging in directly to my PC the cam worked.

The big question...is this camera worth the $50 more than the entry level C920 series camera? For the money you get a ChromaCam program which may or may not work and you get 6 months free xSplit service. Hmmmmm...OBS, which is quite capable, is a free service.

Logitech has so many choices lately, each with increased pricing. Let's face it, it's all about the price. Do you really need your ugly mug put up in a live game? Probably not since it's going to use PC resources that would be better used for gaming. For the $50 extra you could get a couple decent games, or a new mouse, or a mouse pad, or a boat load of peanuts.

The choice is yours.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech C922x Pro + Logitech for Creators Litra Glow - The Ultimate Solution for a Professional Look During Video-Calls

text_fidelity_a:
Philips SHE9850 in-Ear Headphones with Advanced Acoustics (Discontinued by Manufacturer) Some people prefer their headphones outside of their ears, with comfortable ear cushions and other features, such as the [[ASIN:B00007056H Koss KTXPRO1 Titanium Portable Headphones with Volume Control]]. Others prefer wearing their headphones in the privacy of their own ears, with the added bonus of noise isolation.

There are good reasons for choosing either type depending on your personal preferences, such as comfort levels, where and when you're using them, what you're listening to, and whether or not you have to share with other people.

For general use at home, I use the regular "outie", especially for movies or music with inappropriate language that I'd rather not play in surround sound in the presence of young `uns. I also let my son use it when I'd rather not hear another note from the Jonas Brothers. However, in the wee hours of the morning when the only creature stirring is me, I prefer to use in-ear headphones, which shut out everything except the music.

At work, I hardly ever use headphones due to the telephone ringing off the hook, but at lunchtime I sometimes use the in-ear headphones for peace and quiet. I drive to work, so no headphones are needed for the daily commute.

This is a fairly expensive model, but it's worth every cent if you can safely use headphones that cut out most external noise.

Pros:

1. Really nice packaging, easy to open, simple instruction manual
2. Cool, sleek and compact black metal carrying case included, with a cleaning tool and cable clip as accessories.
3. It comes with three different sizes of rubber caps, and as Goldilocks might say, one is for ears that are big, one's for smaller ears, and one will no doubt be just right. Changing caps is simple too.
4. It also includes a pair of memory foam sleeves that fit so snugly in your ears that you may think they belong there.
5. The caps are washable, once you dry them properly before using them again.
6. The sound is marvelous, clear and true, and there's no need to raise the volume to sonic boom levels.
7. The headphones are clearly marked left and right, and are at an angle for easy insertion and a tight seal
8. Drastically cuts down on external noise

Cons:

1. Unless you're using it for an IPod or other portable device, the cord is too short.
2. May feel a bit weird for some people due to the superior noise isolation.
3. You may experience "ewwwwwwwwwww" moments when your friends grab them and try them on. These aren't for sharing.
4. Try saying "in-ear headphones" out loud six times

If you're looking for an excellent pair of (deep breath) in-ear headphones, I think you'll be pleased with this one.

Amanda Richards, July 2, 2008
text_fidelity_b: Philips SHE9850 in-Ear Headphones with Advanced Acoustics (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

For the most part, the 10mm is pretty much useless, as the field of vision is so narrow that constant adjustments need to be made. I decided to give the Expanse series a try. This eyepiece is by far the best in the of the 4. Near Detroit, the light pollution is pretty bad. Viewing the plants and the moon is usually OK. My previous higher powered eyepieces usually made things look really bright and blurry. The Orion Nebula is usually a grey smudge. With the 9mm Expanse, I was able to see more shape to the cloud, and even a handful of stars in its heart. Cloud bands on Jupiter never looked better! I was also able to get a significant amount more detail on the moons surface than what I am used to. Looking at the sun was uneventful today -- only two sunspots.

Ultimately, this is definitely worth buying!

text_fidelity_a:
SAMSUNG (MB-ME32GA/AM) 32GB 95MB/s (U1) microSDHC EVO Select Memory Card with Full-Size Adapter So far so good on this micro sD card.

This is the third micro sD card I’ve bought for my phones since October 2015.

The other two were the 32GB EVO Class 10 Micro SDHC up to 48MB/s with Adapter (MB-MP32DA/AM). And, I was definitely elated to see those were no longer available. Sorry that it is mean-spirited, but after knowing why – I think anyone would be happy to see a fault product go away.

Why did I choose this one?

I purchased the 32GB EVO Class 10 Micro SDHC up to 48MB/s with Adapter (MB-MP32DA/AM) in October of 2015 for my Samsung GS4, and only two (2) months later – I needed a brand new one. Why? It failed. No warning, nothing. Just a failure. The phone wasn’t dropped, shocked, or smashed. It had NO water damage either.

And this wouldn’t be the first failure either for that particular model.

The sD card I bought in December failed as well, but I’ll give it up for it – It went OVER three (3) years before failing. It failed April 3, 2019. I remember that because of the event it failed during. I would’ve expected the failure when I transferred the sD card from the S4 to the S8 in May 2018, but the card still worked.

There were no signs of pending failure or issues. The night before (4/2), it worked and I was able to retrieve some photos off of it.

My mother and I went to Knott’s Berry Farm for the Boysenberry Festival. And, any photos take before we left – GONE. No error messages – just gone. I didn’t know until I got home.

What photos I have were the return photos from the drive home. I had briefly glanced at the card data (on my phone) at about 2pm, but after that (without being dropped, banged, over-heated) the card failed. I know some will ask why I didn’t back them up – I was in transit, driving on the freeway, so it wasn’t feasible.

All I know is that my photos were gone. Again, the phone wasn’t dropped, smashed, shocked. Also, no water damage.

So, I had to purchase another sD card for my phone. This time I chose this one – Samsung 32GB 95MB/s (U1) MicroSD EVO Select Memory Card with Adapter (MB-ME32GA/AM).

From April 2019 to the date of this review, it’s been pretty solid. Though I’m not taking any chances. I also store photos to my S8’s internal storage as well as the sD card.

As far as recommending this one – so far it’s working and has been for over five (5) months, so I’ll recommend it for now.

I’ll update the review if things change.
text_fidelity_b: SAMSUNG (MB-ME32GA/AM) 32GB 95MB/s (U1) microSDHC EVO Select Memory Card with Full-Size Adapter

text_fidelity_a:
iHome 2-In-1 Pen Stylus for iPad/iPad 2 and all Touch Screen Devices (IH-IP2202) I expect that no one is going to use a stylus 100% of the time with their touch screen. There are, however, some times when a stylus is more convenient than using your finger. Drawing objects freehand is a common example. Another example is when you need to precisely move objects around the screen (eg in a CAD program) and this is difficult with your finger because your finger blocks your view of the target area.

There are many many touch screen stylus for sale on Amazon. Some cost less than 50 cents each. All the latest stylus have similar round soft touch rubber tips. All seem to work about the same. This iHome stylus doesn't seem to work any better than the others that I have tried.

The iHome stylus is better looking than most of the competition because of the long slim shape with silver-tone accents. Some of the cheap ones look very plasticy (though they do work just as well). Some other stylus are fatter, which makes them easier to grip if you have large hands.

The built-in ball-point pen is a feature that most other stylus do not have. The pen works well, though I do not know how easy ink refills will be to find. There is no literature in the package about what refills it can use.

Is this product worth $15? I have to say no, but I'm a cheapskate. You can decide on value for yourself, but look at the competition first.
text_fidelity_b: iHome 2-In-1 Pen Stylus for iPad/iPad 2 and all Touch Screen Devices (IH-IP2202)
